extracted.intended_audience: reformers, political thinkers, students of American democracy and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging political reform movements and individual reformers in the American democratic context; emphasizes institutional diagnosis, coherence between principle and program, and the need for national responsibility and intellectual rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform as reconstruction, not restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reform does not mean merely restoring earlier conditions; 'reform does not and cannot mean restoration, it is bound to mean reconstruction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration would 'compromise much that is good in the present' and fail to recover past goods; a mere 'purification' might destroy good with evil and only postpone the tendency toward individual aggrandizement. Effective reform requires rebuilding institutions on better foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address institutional ideas and laws, not only morals
rubrics_metrics.description: The prevailing preconception that an increase of moral energy and some minor legal changes will restore balance is 'less than half true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unscrupulous actors and public moral indifference are mutually reinforcing because of traditional ideas and institutions. Many abuses are encouraged by 'the laws themselves' and by 'the group of ideas and traditional practices behind the laws.' Hence reforms must change underlying institutions and ideas, not merely moral exhortation or enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnose systemic causes rather than treating abuses as neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: Abuses are not merely weeds sprung from neglect but 'cultivated plants' encouraged by traditional methods of cultivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers must recognize how institutional frameworks and cultural ideas foster abuses; eradication requires changing cultivation practices (i.e., institutions and norms), not just punishing individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform requires intellectual as well as moral challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reform must necessarily mean an intellectual as well as a moral challenge; and its higher purposes will never be accomplished unless it is accompanied by a masterful and jubilant intellectual awakening.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform exclusively as moral protest is condemned to sterility; reformers must critique foundational ideas and develop positive political principles, not merely repeat sacrosanct phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question sacred political formulas (e.g., 'equal rights')
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle 'equal rights for all and special privileges for none' is widely accepted but may be 'partly responsible for some of the existing abuses' and is 'only a partial and poverty-stricken statement of the purpose of a democratic polity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should not piously reiterate consecrated phrases without examining whether those principles are safe or sufficient platforms for reform; foundational principles must be critiqued and possibly revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assert national responsibility; abandon Jeffersonian non-interference
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Reform is both meaningless and powerless unless the Jeffersonian principle of non-interference is abandoned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many problems are national in scope and demand 'an exercise of the powers of the central government.' The automatic harmony of individual and public interest is an illusion; public interference sufficient to accomplish public purposes is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor responsible representative government and institutional leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The logic of its purposes will compel [some reformers] to favor the principle of responsible representative government, and it will seek to forge institutions which will endow responsible political government with renewed life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should aim to create institutions that give official leadership genuine responsibility and capability, countering tendencies that undermine representative leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate national political responsibility (Hamiltonian) with democratic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Reformers should look 'in the direction of a much more trustworthy and serviceable political principle' by uniting 'the Hamiltonian principle of national political responsibility and efficiency with a frank democratic purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies rejecting parts of the Jeffersonian creed while transforming Hamiltonianism into a democratic principle—i.e., using centralized power for democratic ends rather than abandoning national capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between principles and practical program
rubrics_metrics.description: A reformer must adapt general political theories to actual political programmes; incoherence undermines effectiveness (illustrated by Bryan's advocacy of Federal power combined with distrust of centralization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals must be logically carried through—e.g., you cannot advocate extensive federal authority and then qualify it in ways that negate its effectiveness. Public opinion will not take inconsistent programmes seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anti-nationalism if seeking national leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti-national positions disqualify a reformer from effective leadership: 'In the campaign of 1900 Mr. Bryan committed himself ... to an anti-national point of view ... and his anti-nationalism has disqualified him for effective leadership.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective national reform requires willingness to assert and trust national institutions and national interest; reflexive opposition to national organization undermines reform capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must provide concrete remedial measures, not only moral claims
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A reformer must identify a particular group of remedial measures with his public personality'—honesty alone is insufficient as a platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public has a right to know specific ways a reformer's righteousness will be made effective; claiming moral superiority without programmatic specifics is politically inept and ineffectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual virtues: candor, consistency, recognition of facts, plain speaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective reform requires intellectual candor, consistency, and a clear recognition of facts; plain speaking and 'intellectual veracity' are praised (e.g., William Travers Jerome's contribution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These virtues combat hypocrisy and administrative lying; they are more than rhetorical traits—they are essential to diagnosing problems and persuading the public to accept institutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public mindset and administrative honesty must be reformed
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal reform 'will never attain its ends until the public ... is converted to an abandonment of ... administrative lying.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform must address social habits, public hypocrisy, and the civic culture that tolerates unenforceable or hypocritical statutes; otherwise legal changes will be subverted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-appropriate program and adaptation to arena (local vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: Success in municipal politics does not automatically scale to state/national politics; a reformer must have distinctive ideas and programmes suitable to the arena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform consisting merely of personal honesty ('his oath of office') is persuasive locally but insufficient nationally; national campaigns require concrete, scalable policies and leadership on issues of national scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept organization, expert skill, and administrative specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: The text criticizes the 'old Democratic dislike of organization' and argues reformers must have 'faith in the ability of the national political organization to promote the national welfare.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should not denigrate expert administration or organizational competence; institutional competence and specialization are necessary to execute large-scale reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sacrificing exceptional ability to the popular average
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Confidence in the average man ... means to Mr. Bryan an utter lack of faith in those personal instruments whereby such rule can be endowed with foresight, moderation, and direction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing only the average and mistrusting exceptional leaders or organizations risks democratic degeneration; reforms should preserve avenues for exceptional leadership within democratic accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate rhetorical methods and populist tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressive popular agitation and 'yellow journalism' style appeals (e.g., Hearst) frame reform in purely populist terms—using 'equal rights' rhetoric while disclaiming socialism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a reformer's methods rely on manipulative popular catchwords and spectacle rather than substantive policy proposals; unscrupulous populism can mask lack of coherent program.
